- When sentiment is consistently high (≥0.8) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.2) or negative, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to account for risk aversion or market panic.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > true by >5%), model often overcorrects in next period; apply a “lag correction” — reduce forecast by 2–5% in following 2–3 periods.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (price drops after peak or rises after trough), model tends to hold trend; adjust forecast to align with 3–5 period moving average of history.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the forecast window; apply a “horizon decay” — reduce forecast by 0.5–1% per 5-day segment toward end of horizon.
- If sentiment history shows sudden shift from positive to negative, model often fails to adjust quickly; apply a “sentiment lag” — delay forecast adjustment by 1–2 periods if sentiment drops sharply.
